content.title: About
content.content: Unenriched whole wheat flour is milled from the entire wheat kernel, retaining the bran, germ, and endosperm. It has a richer flavor, darker color, and higher levels of fiber, vitamins, and minerals compared with refined white flour.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole wheat flour keeps all parts of the grain: bran, germ, and endosperm.
It contains two to three times more dietary fiber than white flour.
Unlike many refined flours, unenriched whole wheat flour is not fortified with iron, folic acid, or B‑vitamins.
Dough made with whole wheat flour usually requires longer mixing and proofing times.
The color of baked goods can range from light brown to almost black, depending on the wheat variety.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestive health, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: B‑vitamin content
items.content: Whole wheat flour provides thiamine, niacin, and folate, which are important for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Rich in minerals
items.content: It supplies magnesium, iron, zinc, and selenium, essential for muscle function, immunity, and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Lower glycemic index
items.content: Compared with white flour, whole wheat has a slower carbohydrate absorption rate, beneficial for weight management and glucose control.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Bran and germ contain phenolic compounds that help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Wheat allergy or celiac disease
items.content: People with wheat allergy or celiac disease should avoid whole wheat flour as it can trigger severe reactions.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can bind minerals and reduce their absorption; soaking or fermenting dough can mitigate this effect.

items.title: Shelf‑life
items.content: Because the germ contains oils, whole wheat flour can become rancid more quickly; store it refrigerated or frozen for longer freshness.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Use the flour for breads, rolls, flatbreads, pancakes, muffins, and cookies. When substituting for white flour, increase liquid slightly and allow the dough extra resting time.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the flour in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For extended storage, refrigerate or freeze to prevent the oils from turning rancid.
